{{short description|Study of subsets of integers and behavior under addition}}
'''Additive number theory''' is the subfield of [[number theory]] concerning the study of subsets of [[integer]]s and their behavior under [[addition]]. More abstractly, the field of additive number theory includes the study of [[abelian group]]s and [[commutative semigroup]]s with an operation of addition. Additive number theory has close ties to [[combinatorial number theory]] and the [[geometry of numbers]]. Principal objects of study include the [[sumset]] of two subsets {{Mvar|A}} and {{Mvar|B}} of elements from an abelian group {{Mvar|G}},

:<math>A + B = \{a+b : a \in A, b \in B\},</math>

and the {{Mvar|h}}-fold sumset of {{Mvar|A}}, 

:<math>hA = \underset{h}{\underbrace{A + \cdots + A}}\,.</math>

==Additive number theory==
The field is principally devoted to consideration of ''direct problems'' over (typically) the integers, that is, determining the structure of {{Math|''hA''}} from the structure of {{Mvar|A}}: for example, determining which elements can be represented as a sum from {{Math|''hA''}}, where ''{{Mvar|A}}'' is a fixed subset.<ref>Nathanson (1996) II:1</ref> Two classical problems of this type are the [[Goldbach conjecture]] (which is the conjecture that {{Math|2&primes;}} contains all even numbers greater than two, where {{Math|&primes;}} is the set of [[Prime number|primes]]) and [[Waring's problem]] (which asks how large must ''{{Mvar|h}}'' be to guarantee that {{Math|''hA<sub>k</sub>''}} contains all positive integers, where 

:<math>A_k=\{0^k,1^k,2^k,3^k,\ldots\}</math> 

is the set of {{Mvar|k}}th powers). Many of these problems are studied using the tools from the [[Hardy-Littlewood circle method]] and from [[sieve theory|sieve methods]].  For example, Vinogradov proved that every sufficiently large odd number is the sum of three primes, and so every sufficiently large even integer is the sum of four primes.  [[David Hilbert|Hilbert]] proved that, for every integer {{Math|''k'' > 1}}, every non-negative integer is the sum of a bounded number of {{Mvar|k}}th powers.  In general, a set ''{{Mvar|A}}'' of nonnegative integers is called a ''basis'' of order ''{{Mvar|h}}'' if {{Math|''hA''}} contains all positive integers, and it is called an ''asymptotic basis'' if {{Math|''hA''}} contains all sufficiently large integers.  Much current research in this area concerns properties of general asymptotic bases of finite order.  For example, a set ''{{Mvar|A}}'' is called a ''minimal asymptotic basis'' of order ''{{Mvar|h}}'' if ''{{Mvar|A}}'' is an asymptotic basis of order {{Mvar|h}} but no proper subset of ''{{Mvar|A}}'' is an asymptotic basis of order ''{{Mvar|h}}''.  It has been proved that minimal asymptotic bases of order ''{{Mvar|h}}'' exist for all ''{{Mvar|h}}'', and that there also exist asymptotic bases of order ''{{Mvar|h}}'' that contain no minimal asymptotic bases of order ''{{Mvar|h}}''. Another question to be considered is how small can the number of representations of {{Mvar|n}} as a sum of ''{{Mvar|h}}'' elements in an asymptotic basis can be. This is the content of the [[Erdős–Turán conjecture on additive bases]].
